Below is a structured comparison of two widely used instructional design models—ADDIE and the Dick & Carey (Systems Approach) model—covering their origins, phases, evaluation emphases, flexibility, and typical use contexts.

Overview and Origins
- ADDIE: ADDIE stands for Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation, and is a well-known framework that outlines generic processes of systematic instructional design across five phases; it is often described as a “family of models” with widespread use and adaptation across fields, originating at Florida State University in 1975 and evolving into an instructional system design approach used for building training and performance-support tools <cite id="8987ff0a-0">The ADDIE model is an instructional design framework that comprises five phases: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">In the context of education, the ADDIE model is a well-known model that outlines generic processes of systematic instructional design</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-3">Often described as a "family of models" due to shared foundational principles, the ADDIE model does not have a single original author or a universally accepted definition, despite its widespread use across various fields</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-4">The ADDIE model has become influential since its inception at Florida State University in 1975</cite> <cite id="610af835-1">Another well-documented model is the ADDIE model, an instructional system design framework that has been used by many designers and course developers</cite>.
- Dick & Carey: The Dick & Carey model was first developed in 1968 at Florida State University and has been published in multiple editions (1978, 1985, 1990, 1996) as The Systematic Design of Instruction; it is a goal-oriented, procedural, systems-based approach that emphasizes comprehensive planning and design of instruction <cite id="610af835-1">Regarding the Dick-and-Carey instructional design model, its first version was developed in 1968 at Florida State University</cite> <cite id="610af835-1">According to Chang (2006), the Dick-and-Carey model uses the system approach for designing effective instructions</cite> <cite id="610af835-2">The Dick & Carey model is a nine or 10 step process for planning and designing effective learning initiatives</cite>.

Phases and Components
- ADDIE phases and activities: Analysis identifies needs, resources, and constraints; Design specifies learning objectives and evaluation tools; Development creates content and pilot tests; Implementation delivers instruction; Evaluation integrates formative checks at each stage and a summative assessment at the end; the process is iterative, allowing returns to prior steps based on evaluation feedback <cite id="8987ff0a-0">During the analysis phase, educational objectives are established, and evaluation tools are devised; during the development phase, educational program content is generated and pilot-tested; during the implementation phase, the program is delivered; during the evaluation phase, all aspects are assessed</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">Formative evaluation occurs at each stage; summative evaluation is conducted at the end of the project</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-4">It is an iterative instructional design method in which the instructional designer may return to any previous step based on formative evaluation; the result of one phase serves as the starting point for the next</cite>.
- Dick & Carey steps: Commonly summarized as nine steps (sometimes ten) including (1) identify instructional goals, (2) conduct instructional analysis, (3) identify entry behaviors and learner characteristics, (4) write performance objectives, (5) develop criterion-referenced test items, (6) develop instructional strategy, (7) develop and select instructional materials, (8) design and conduct formative evaluation, and (9) revise instruction; a summative evaluation is conducted after implementation, often by an independent evaluator <cite id="2f479424-3">The Dick and Carey instructional design model provides a systematic design of instruction using the nine-steps ... namely identify instructional goal ... write performance objectives ... develop criterion-referenced test items ... develop instructional strategy ... develop and select instructional materials ... design and conduct formative evaluation ... and revise instruction</cite> <cite id="2f479424-4">The following are ten steps or stages ... 1) Identifying goals ... 2) Instructional analysis ... 3) Identifying entry behaviors and learner characteristics ... 4) Writing performance objectives ... 5) Developing criterion-referenced test items ... 6) Developing instructional strategy ... 7) Developing and selecting instructional materials ... 8) Designing and conducting formative evaluation ... 9) Revising instruction ... 10) Conducting summative evaluation</cite> <cite id="2f479424-2">The Dick and Carey model ... has nine sequential processes ... includes a feedback loop ... and emphasizes learner-centred instruction</cite>.
- Relationship between models: Dick & Carey’s model includes all five stages of ADDIE but adds further depth and structure, particularly in design and assessment; ADDIE is often used to guide development toward a product that serves learner needs, with overlapping phases that must incorporate a learning theory to remain flexible <cite id="610af835-2">This model does include all five stages of the ADDIE model, but it also adds further depth and structure</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-0">The ADDIE model is an instructional design framework that comprises five phases</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-3">It guides the development process toward a product that serves the needs of the learner; sometimes overlap; phases can be interrelated but must incorporate a learning theory</cite>.

Learner and Task Emphasis
- Both models begin with learner-focused analyses: Dick & Carey explicitly integrates learner characteristics, entry behaviors, and context (with separate instructional and learner analyses) to tailor goals and objectives, and develops criterion-referenced assessments aligned to those objectives <cite id="2f479424-0">An instructional analysis is conducted to determine the knowledge and skills learners need ... complemented by an analysis of learner characteristics and the learning context ... specific and measurable performance objectives are written ... assessment instruments are developed to measure the extent to which these objectives are met</cite> <cite id="2f479424-3">Conduct instructional analysis ... identify entry-level behaviours ... write performance objectives ... developing criterion-referenced test items</cite>.
- ADDIE also conducts analysis to define goals and resources; formative evaluation at each phase supports learner-centered refinement, and summative evaluation at the end checks instructional effectiveness <cite id="8987ff0a-1">The analysis phase involves identifying the learning problem, user needs, existing knowledge, and defining goals and objectives</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">Formative evaluation occurs at each stage ... A summative evaluation is conducted at the end of the project</cite>.

Evaluation Strategy
- ADDIE: Dual-evaluation emphasis—formative evaluation at each phase enables early intervention and iterative improvement; summative evaluation at program end assesses overall effectiveness and alignment to goals <cite id="8987ff0a-1">Formative and summative processes ... Formative evaluation occurs at each stage ... A summative evaluation is conducted at the end of the project</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-4">Two types of evaluation need to be undertaken ... formative evaluation ... and summative evaluation which assesss the actual value of the whole instructional design at the end</cite>.
- Dick & Carey: Embedded assessment and feedback loops. The model builds assessment frameworks from the outset (criterion-referenced test items aligned to objectives) and integrates formative evaluation and revision as a core loop; summative evaluation is conducted post-implementation, ideally by an independent evaluator to maintain objectivity <cite id="610af835-0">A crucial component of the Dick and Carey model ... development of an assessment framework to evaluate training</cite> <cite id="2f479424-0">Assessment instruments are then developed to measure the extent to which these objectives are met ... Formative evaluation is carried out throughout the development process to gather feedback, allowing for continuous refinement</cite> <cite id="2f479424-4">Designing and conducting formative evaluation ... Revising instruction ... Conducting summative evaluation ... evaluated by an independent evaluator</cite>.

Flexibility and Iteration
- ADDIE: Process-based and iterative across phases; designers can return to prior steps based on formative evaluation, supporting continuous refinement during development and implementation, though traditionally framed in five sequential phases <cite id="8987ff0a-4">It is an iterative instructional design method in which the instructional designer may return to any previous step based on formative evaluation</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-0">The developed program is delivered to the target audience during the implementation phase. During the evaluation phase, all aspects of education before and after its application are assessed</cite>.
- Dick & Carey: Nine-step, systems-based process that explicitly incorporates a feedback loop and ongoing revision; emphasizes iterative development through continuous refinement of instructions, with a stronger focus on design processes than on implementation details <cite id="610af835-0">One notable update to the Dick and Carey model is the inclusion of a feedback loop, which allows for continuous improvement and refinement of the instructional design</cite> <cite id="610af835-2">The Dick and Carey model ... includes all five stages of the ADDIE model ... adds further depth and structure ... and focuses on design and less on implementation than the ADDIE model</cite> <cite id="2f479424-2">The model ... has nine sequential processes ... includes a feedback loop ... emphasizes learner-centred instruction</cite>.

Scope and Artifacts
- ADDIE deliverables span needs analysis documents, objectives and storyboards (design), prototypes and developed content (development), delivery plans and training (implementation), and evaluation instruments and reports (formative and summative) <cite id="8987ff0a-0">During the design phase, educational objectives are established, and evaluation tools are devised ... During the development phase, educational program content is generated and pilot-tested ... During the evaluation phase, all aspects of education before and after its application are assessed</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">The design phase is a process of specifying learning objectives systematically, often with storyboards and prototypes ... implementation develops and applies a procedure ... evaluation consists of formative and summative processes</cite>.
- Dick & Carey artifacts include clearly stated instructional goals, detailed instructional and learner analyses, performance objectives, criterion-referenced tests, instructional strategies and materials, formative evaluation plans, revision logs, and independent summative evaluations <cite id="2f479424-3">Identify instructional goal ... instructional analysis ... write performance objectives ... develop criterion-referenced test items ... develop instructional strategy ... materials ... design and conduct formative evaluation ... and revise instruction</cite> <cite id="2f479424-4">Developing criterion-referenced test items ... Developing and selecting instructional materials ... Formative evaluation ... Revising instruction ... Conducting summative evaluation by an independent evaluator</cite>.

Use Contexts and Strengths
- ADDIE strengths: Broadly applicable, structured, and easy to adapt across training and performance-support projects; its phase-gate approach and explicit evaluation loops support systematic build-test-learn cycles in diverse settings (online courses, healthcare training, corporate e-learning) while remaining iterative and reflective <cite id="8987ff0a-3">This model serves as a fundamental tool in instructional design, providing a systematic five-stage process</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-4">The process-based model enables instructional designers ... to produce efficient and effective teaching practices</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-0">Used to create continuing online training programs for nurses ... educational applications ... design constructivist learning modules</cite> <cite id="610af835-0">ADDIE focuses on the systematic development of effective instructional materials and emphasises iterative feedback loops</cite>.
- Dick & Carey strengths: Comprehensive planning for complex instruction with strong alignment (goals→analysis→objectives→assessment→strategy/materials), making it well-suited where deep design quality assurance and criterion-referenced measurement are critical; its systems approach and explicit feedback/revision mechanisms support robust quality control and transfer to practice <cite id="610af835-1">The Dick-and-Carey model uses the system approach for designing effective instructions</cite> <cite id="2f479424-0">Assessment instruments are then developed to measure the extent to which these objectives are met, ensuring validity and reliability</cite> <cite id="2f479424-2">The model has undergone several updates ... inclusion of a feedback loop ... and emphasises learner-centred instruction</cite> <cite id="610af835-2">This model does include all five stages of the ADDIE model, but it also adds further depth and structure</cite>.

Key Differences (Head-to-Head)
- Emphasis and sequencing: Dick & Carey is a nine-step, systems-driven design process with explicit feedback/revision loops and deep integration of assessment; ADDIE is a five-phase ID framework used to build and evaluate training/performance support, with overlapping, iterative phases and reflective checkpoints <cite id="2f479424-3">The Dick and Carey model provides a systematic design of instruction using the nine-steps</cite> <cite id="2f479424-4">Formative evaluation ... Revising instruction ... Summative evaluation</cite> <cite id="610af835-0">The Dick and Carey model ... leads to the evaluation of teaching and outlines instructional goals</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">ADDIE ... formative and summative processes</cite>.
- Focus: Dick & Carey focuses more on design and quality assurance (detailed analyses, criterion-referenced tests, strategy and materials design), whereas ADDIE balances design with implementation and delivery considerations, often guiding development toward usable products for learners <cite id="610af835-2">This model ... adds further depth and structure ... and focuses on design and less on implementation than the ADDIE model</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-3">ADDIE ... provides a structured approach ... to identify learning needs, design engaging content, develop appropriate assessments, implement instruction, and evaluate its effectiveness</cite>.
- Evaluation and control: Dick & Carey embeds assessment framework development early and mandates iterative formative evaluation and revision; ADDIE emphasizes formative checks across phases and a summative evaluation at the end to judge overall effectiveness <cite id="610af835-0">A crucial component ... development of an assessment framework to evaluate training</cite> <cite id="2f479424-0">Formative evaluation is carried out throughout the development process to gather feedback, allowing for continuous refinement</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">Formative evaluation occurs at each stage ... A summative evaluation is conducted at the end of the project</cite>.
- Roots and philosophy: Both models are rooted in behaviorist-positivist traditions, prioritizing teacher-centered instruction and systematic sequencing of stages to achieve specified outcomes; however, they are among the most widely recognized models in instructional design and instructional technology <cite id="610af835-4">Both instructional models were developed as a direct outcome of the behaviourism movement ... and currently stand as two of the most widely recognised instructional design models</cite>.

When to Use Which
- Choose ADDIE when you need a pragmatic, phase-gated process to develop and deploy training or performance support across analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation, with built-in reflection at each step and flexibility to iterate without discarding prior work <cite id="8987ff0a-0">The ADDIE model ... comprises five phases</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-4">Iterative ... may return to any previous step based on formative evaluation</cite>.
- Choose Dick & Carey when deep, criterion-referenced design and quality assurance are priorities—for complex programs requiring rigorous alignment from goals to assessments, materials, and revision cycles—with explicit feedback loops and independent summative evaluation for validity and transfer <cite id="610af835-1">The Dick-and-Carey model uses the system approach for designing effective instructions</cite> <cite id="2f479424-3">Develop criterion-referenced test items ... develop and select instructional materials ... design and conduct formative evaluation ... and revise instruction</cite> <cite id="2f479424-4">Conducting summative evaluation ... evaluated by an independent evaluator</cite>.

Summary
- ADDIE and Dick & Carey are complementary, process-based models. Dick & Carey’s systems approach adds depth and structure over the five ADDIE phases, with stronger upfront and continuous alignment (analysis→objectives→assessment→strategy/materials→revision) and formal feedback loops; ADDIE provides a widely adopted, iterative, end-to-end framework emphasizing formative checkpoints and summative judgment, and is frequently used to guide practical development and implementation into performance support <cite id="8987ff0a-0">The ADDIE model is an instructional design framework that comprises five phases</cite> <cite id="8987ff0a-1">Formative ... and summative processes</cite> <cite id="610af835-2">Dick & Carey ... includes all five stages of the ADDIE model, but it also adds further depth and structure</cite> <cite id="610af835-1">The Dick-and-Carey model uses the system approach for designing effective instructions</cite> <cite id="610af835-0">ADDIE focuses on the systematic development of effective instructional materials and emphasises iterative feedback loops</cite>.

This process-based model enables instructional designers, content developers, and even teachers to produce efficient and effective teaching practices. The ADDIE model consists of five phases: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation (see Fig. 1a). In this approach, the result of one phase serves as the starting point for the next one (Aldoobie, 2015). 

The analysis phase in the ADDIE model defines, identifies, and determines the feasible solutions to a problem (Kulvietiene & Sileikiene, 2006). The design phase is primarily concerned with implementing the directives that the designer received from the analysis phase. Additionally, throughout the design phase, the instructional designer concentrates on choosing a course format and designing an appropriate instructional approach and assessment technique for the subject (Aldoobie, 2015). Based on the design phase, the development phase aggregates all the separate pieces to create a complete working prototype ready for implementation. Often, instructional designers argue that the components envisioned in the design phase must "come to life" in the development phase (Onguko et al., 2013). The implementation phase is concerned with transacting a plan; it entails three primary steps: training, preparing learners, and structuring the learning environment. Evaluation is the final step of the ADDIE model. The evaluation phase checks each step of the instructional design to ensure that they are aligned with the program's intended goals. Two types of evaluation need to be undertaken in the ADDIE model. The first one is a formative evaluation, which can be undertaken after completing each phase. Summary answer
- If your two‑week corporate compliance training must be high‑quality with minimal early evaluation cycles, Dick & Carey’s Systems Approach is generally more appropriate because it is designed for iterative, feedback‑driven improvement while keeping design tightly coupled to measurable outcomes; within a tight schedule you can run lightweight, job‑embedded formative checks (e.g., SME reviews, task‑analysis spot checks) rather than building a full quiz matrix, and its performance‑focused analysis helps ensure content maps to required competencies and tasks <cite id="8b73cd03-0">Dick & Carey’s Systems Approach is a nine or ten‑step process that includes all five stages of ADDIE plus further depth and structure and emphasizes iterative revision and ongoing feedback loops</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">Dick & Carey provides a goal‑oriented, procedural structure with explicit instructional goals and a feedback loop enabling continuous improvement and learner‑centred refinement</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C is a procedural system with ten process components where each component is linked to outcomes, focusing on what learners must know/do and ensuring the instructional strategy is empirically grounded and replicable</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">D&C accommodates emerging technologies and constraints, with performance analysis revealing needs and enabling efficient, cost‑effective combinations of media and methods</cite>.  
- If you prefer strict stage-gate discipline and documentation for auditability and regulatory alignment, ADDIE’s linear phases and explicit emphasis on formative evaluation can be adapted, but you will need to compress or substitute formative testing with targeted checkpoints; its structured analysis and evaluation phases help mitigate risk, though its linear flow may be less nimble under a two‑week deadline <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE is a five‑stage model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation) that systematically develops effective materials with iterative feedback loops and reflection/revision at each stage</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-4">Both ADDIE and Dick & Carey are behaviourist‑positivist models emphasizing teacher‑centred instruction and systematic stages with reflection, critique, and potential revision</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-3">ADDIE is often described as developed by Dick & Carey to improve instructional systems with five stages</cite>.

Why Dick & Carey tends to fit a 2‑week compliance project with no formative testing budget
- Built‑in feedback loops and goal‑first design reduce the need for heavy iterative quizzes: D&C starts from explicit performance outcomes and links instructional strategies to those outcomes, with dedicated assessment frameworks and feedback loops for continuous improvement; this lets you validate design quality through outcome alignment and targeted reviews rather than extensive formative quizzes alone <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C specifies instructional goals and includes a feedback loop for continuous improvement; ADDIE emphasizes iterative feedback and reflection</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">Each system component is linked to desired outcomes, ensuring strategies and outcomes are empirically connected</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">A crucial component is an assessment framework to evaluate training and identify enhancements</cite>.  
- Rapid iteration without losing structure: While often taught as a linear sequence, D&C is used as a “systems” approach where steps can be cycled and components revisited; in a two‑week sprint, you can iterate on task analyses, scenario design, and delivery options while keeping alignment to outcomes and mandated competencies <cite id="8b73cd03-0">D&C includes all five ADDIE stages plus added depth; it emphasizes iterative development through ongoing revision</cite> <cite id="b721193d-3">Dick & Carey’s approach can be applied with steps that can be skipped or cycled in planning and development processes</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">The system allows components to remain current by accommodating new constraints/technologies, making it adaptable to time and tooling limits</cite>.  
- Compliance risk mitigation via performance analysis: D&C’s strong emphasis on performance analysis and learner/context analysis ensures training content and scenarios reflect regulatory tasks and constraints; you can prioritize mandated competencies and job‑embedded assessments (e.g., role‑plays, checklists, case decisions) even without a quiz budget, while still meeting auditability needs through outcome statements and evidence logs <cite id="b721193d-2">Performance analysis identifies skills and processes to achieve instructional goals; learner analysis determines context and appropriate strategies and evaluation</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C advocates a systems approach because each component is linked to learner outcomes and instructional strategies, focusing on what learners must know/do at instruction end</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">Performance analysis and learner analysis reveal needs, constraints, and technologies, enabling efficient media/teaching method combinations</cite>.  
- Practical fit when formative testing is off‑limits: With no budget for formative quizzes, D&C’s design emphasizes document‑ed goals, SME‑reviewed task lists, and pre‑implementation walkthroughs as primary quality gates; its assessment phase also provides templates for spot‑checking and summative evidence (e.g., observation rubrics for simulations) that fit compliance records <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C includes formative evaluation planning and a summative evaluation improvement loop</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">The model’s assessment framework identifies necessary enhancements and modifications to instruction</cite>.

Why ADDIE can work (with adaptations) even without formative testing
- Stage‑wise rigor and documentation align to compliance audits: ADDIE’s formal phases and emphasis on analysis, design, and evaluation lend themselves to clear documentation trails (needs/risks, competency mapping, design decisions, and evaluations), which are valuable in regulated environments; within a two‑week sprint, you can preserve auditability by focusing evaluation on spot checks and proxy measures instead of continuous quizzes <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE provides a structured approach for identifying learning needs, designing content, developing assessments, implementing, and evaluating effectiveness</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-4">ADDIE emphasizes reflection, critique, and potential revision at conception, development, and deployment</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-3">ADDIE aims to improve instructional systems through analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation</cite>.  
- Compress formative evaluation into checkpoints: Though ADDIE names formative evaluation explicitly, you can substitute or compress it—e.g., targeted SME reviews at Analysis→Design handoff, design pattern libraries for compliance scenarios, and “paper‑prototyping” of key cases—then run limited live spot checks during Implementation; its feedback loops still enforce revision cycles without a quiz budget <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE emphasizes iterative feedback loops throughout design and implementation</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-1">ADDIE’s detailed analysis and development steps align well when content requires clear instructional goals and continuous refinement based on assessments and feedback</cite>.

Head‑to‑head trade‑offs for your constraints
- Speed and adaptability: Dick & Carey’s systems approach and feedback loops support rapid, outcome‑aligned iteration; it is well‑suited to time‑boxed sprints and environments where the “right” tasks and measures can be clarified mid‑stream <cite id="8b73cd03-0">D&C adds depth and iterative revision beyond ADDIE’s five stages</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C’s linkage of strategies to outcomes and focus on what learners must accomplish at the end support iterative refinement</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">D&C remains current by accommodating constraints and technologies; instructional delivery options enable efficient and cost‑effective combinations</cite>.  
- Process control and audit: ADDIE’s linear phase gates and explicit evaluation phases produce thorough documentation; with a tight budget for formative testing, you can still meet audit needs by substituting expert reviews, job aids, and targeted evidence collection for quizzes, while keeping stage gates disciplined <cite id="8b73cd03-3">ADDIE consists of analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation to improve instructional systems</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-2">Its structured phases and feedback loops emphasize systematic development and iterative improvement</cite>.

Practical recommendations under a 2‑week, no‑formative‑testing budget
- Choose Dick & Carey for instructor‑led and blended compliance modules:
  - Week 1: Performance and learner analysis to lock in mandated competencies; formulate explicit outcome statements; design job‑embedded assessment rubrics (role‑plays, checklists, case decisions) and development plans; run SME “fit/coverage” reviews as the main quality gate instead of quizzes <cite id="b721193d-2">Instructional analysis specifies skills, processes, and tasks to achieve learning objectives; learner analysis guides strategy and evaluation</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">Formulate explicit instructional goals and develop an assessment framework to evaluate training and drive improvements</cite>.  
  - Week 2: Build materials (scenario‑based slides, job aids), implement with live facilitators and micro‑coaches, and collect targeted evidence via rubric‑based observations and post‑session reflections; use a lightweight debrief to feed back into the assessment framework <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C’s assessment framework enables identification of enhancements and modifications to the instructional process</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-0">D&C emphasizes iterative development and ongoing revision of instructions</cite>.  
- Use ADDIE if your compliance program requires strict phase documentation and approvals:
  - Analysis: Document compliance requirements, hazards, and competency gaps; freeze scope; define acceptance criteria for each module.  
  - Design/Development: Implement design reviews and pattern reuse to ensure quality; produce SME‑checked scenario libraries; defer or minimize internal quizzes and rely on proxy measures (checklists, traceability matrices) and pre/post observation checklists.  
  - Implementation/Evaluation: Run spot‑checks and sampling of learners; maintain an evidence log mapping each competency to observed performance and corrective actions <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE’s development emphasizes assessments, implementation, and evaluation for effectiveness</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-4">Emphasis on critique and revision at each stage helps maintain quality even with limited testing cycles</cite>.

When to prefer ADDIE over Dick & Carey
- If your organization mandates formal phase approvals, risk boards, and documentation trails (e.g., regulatory change control), ADDIE’s explicit phases and evaluation gates provide a clearer audit trail and structure; ensure that “formative evaluation” is replaced by structured SME reviews and design walkthroughs to meet quality while preserving documentation <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE provides a structured, systematic development process with assessment, implementation, and evaluation</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-3">It aims to improve instructional systems through five defined stages</cite>.  
- For highly linear, step‑by‑step compliance procedures where fidelity matters, ADDIE’s stage‑wise discipline can reduce variance across trainers; compress development with D&C’s feedback loops by using outcome‑aligned checklists and SME “fit” reviews as lightweight formative stand‑ins <cite id="8b73cd03-4">Both models are teacher‑centred, systematic with reflection and revision</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C ensures strategies are empirically linked to outcomes, which can be enforced via checklists/rubrics</cite>.

When to prefer Dick & Carey over ADDIE
- If your compliance content is dynamic (e.g., evolving policies, high ambiguity) and you need to iterate quickly with live learners, D&C’s systems approach and feedback loops let you course‑correct mid‑stream while keeping outcomes anchored; its performance analysis increases regulatory relevance by aligning to actual job tasks and constraints <cite id="8b73cd03-0">D&C adds iterative revision and ongoing feedback beyond ADDIE</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">D&C accommodates new constraints/technologies and enables efficient media/teaching method combinations</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C’s components are linked so instructional strategies and outcomes are aligned</cite>.  
- If your budget constraint is absolute (no quizzes), D&C’s emphasis on assessment frameworks and learner‑centred design enables quality assurance via expert review, scenario walkthroughs, and observation rubrics rather than continuous testing; this often yields acceptable evidence for compliance records while preserving instructional fidelity <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C’s assessment framework identifies needed enhancements; feedback loop enables continuous improvement</cite>.

Evidence on relative effectiveness
- Comparative evidence suggests both models can produce similar learning outcomes and retention when appropriately applied; one study found no significant difference in retention between ADDIE and Dick & Carey–designed instruction in technical training, indicating that with strong design processes either model can be effective <cite id="9e7c8292-0">There was no significant difference in retention scores between Dick & Carey and ADDIE models</cite>.  
- Interest/engagement can vary; another study reported significant differences in interest favoring one model, underscoring the importance of aligning the model to learner context and delivery modality rather than expecting universal superiority <cite id="9e7c8292-2">There was a significant difference in interest scores between Dick & Carey and ADDIE models</cite>.  
- Overall, plan development using Dick & Carey’s systems approach is explicitly organized for producing and improving training, including formative and summative evaluation components, which is valuable when testing cycles are compressed or absent <cite id="9e7c8292-1">Dick & Carey model organizes and produces knowledge, experiences, and projects that lead to improved learning; it includes steps such as planning and generating formative evaluations and reviewing/improving summative evaluations</cite>.

Bottom line
- With a two‑week timeline and no formative testing budget, Dick & Carey (the Dick & Carey Systems Approach) is generally more appropriate for corporate compliance training because its goal‑first, systems design with feedback loops enables rapid, outcome‑aligned iteration using expert reviews and job‑embedded evidence rather than quizzes; it embeds performance analysis to ensure regulatory relevance and provides assessment frameworks for targeted evidence collection <cite id="8b73cd03-0">D&C includes ADDIE stages plus iterative revision and ongoing feedback</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C defines explicit instructional goals, emphasizes learner‑centred design, and includes feedback loops for continuous improvement</cite> <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C ties each component to outcomes and focuses on what learners must know/do</cite> <cite id="b721193d-4">D&C adapts to constraints/technologies and supports efficient, cost‑effective delivery options</cite>.  
- If your organization prioritizes formal documentation and phase approvals over speed, adopt ADDIE and substitute formative testing with rigorous SME reviews, design walkthroughs, and proxy measures; maintain a clear evidence log across Analysis→Evaluation to satisfy compliance while compressing development cycles <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE provides a structured, iterative process with assessment, implementation, and evaluation for effectiveness</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-4">Emphasis on critique/revision at each stage sustains quality without extensive testing</cite>.

Action checklist (budget‑aware)
- Regardless of model, start with performance analysis and regulator‑mandated competencies; freeze scope; define acceptance criteria and evidence types (job aids, checklists, rubrics) <cite id="b721193d-2">Instructional analysis identifies skills and tasks; learner analysis informs strategy and evaluation</cite>.  
- Replace full formative quizzes with: SME “fit/coverage” reviews; paper‑prototype key cases and run dry runs; pre‑delivery design walkthroughs; and observation/rubric‑based spot checks during implementation <cite id="b721193d-0">D&C’s assessment framework guides improvements; feedback loops enable continuous refinement</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE emphasizes iterative feedback loops and structured evaluation</cite>.  
- Ensure each compliance competency maps to at least one observable, job‑embedded assessment with a scoring guide; maintain a traceability matrix linking requirements to assessments and corrective actions <cite id="b721193d-1">D&C links instructional strategies to outcomes through a systematic design</cite> <cite id="9e7c8292-1">D&C’s steps include planning formative evaluations and improving summative evaluations</cite>.  
- Plan a post‑implementation debrief to feed data back into design (e.g., near‑misses, gaps) and adjust materials for future cohorts; this leverages the model’s feedback loops within scarce testing cycles <cite id="8b73cd03-0">Dick & Carey emphasizes ongoing revision of instructions through feedback</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE calls for critique and potential revision at each stage</cite>.

Uncertainties and how to resolve them
- Direct, head‑to‑head evidence in corporate compliance is limited; education/technical training studies show both models can achieve comparable learning outcomes, with contextual factors (audits, content dynamism) often tipping the balance. Pilot a small cohort with either model, collect proxy measures (checklists, rubric scores, time‑to‑proficiency), and compare against your regulatory evidence standards to validate the chosen approach within your timeline and budget <cite id="9e7c8292-0">No significant difference in retention between ADDIE and D&C in technical training</cite> <cite id="9e7c8292-2">Significant differences in interest favoring one model, indicating contextual sensitivity</cite>.  
- If your LMS supports analytics, consider a hybrid: run mandatory pre/post job aids (not learner‑graded quizzes) and log completion/accuracy to serve as lightweight formative evidence; this preserves user experience while meeting accountability needs <cite id="b721193d-4">Instructional delivery options enable efficient and cost‑effective combinations of media and methods</cite>.

In short, pick Dick & Carey to maximize quality per sprint week and proxy‑based evidence; choose ADDIE if your compliance governance demands strict phase artifacts and approvals. Either can work well with a flat formative testing budget if you substitute structured expert reviews, job‑embedded assessments, and observation‑based evidence for quizzes and run a small‑scale post‑launch synthesis to course‑correct rapidly <cite id="8b73cd03-0">Dick & Carey’s systems approach adds iterative depth beyond ADDIE and emphasizes ongoing revision</cite> <cite id="b721193d-0">Its explicit goals and feedback loops support continuous improvement without heavy testing</cite> <cite id="8b73cd03-2">ADDIE’s structured phases and feedback loops ensure systematic quality even with limited testing</cite> <cite id="9e7c8292-1">D&C’s development process includes formative and summative evaluation planning to improve training</cite>.

The ADDIE model, on the other hand, is a widely used instructional design framework that stands for Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation.ADDIE, a behaviourist-positivist ID model, was developed by the Centre for Educational Technology in 1975 for performance-based learning in education, offering a structured approach to instructional design (Branch, 2009).ADDIE focuses on the systematic development of effective instructional materials and emphasises the importance of iterative feedback loops throughout the design process (Molenda, 2003).The ADDIE model provides a structured approach for instructional designers to identify learning needs, design engaging content, develop appropriate assessments, implement instruction, and evaluate its effectiveness.

Instructional goals are defined through a systematic approach that involves addressing specific problems, goal clarity, and available resources (Dick & Carey, 2009;Seel et al., 2017).The process starts by identifying the learner's desired skills and knowledge, and then it conducts a thorough analysis of the learners and linguistic contexts to produce performance assessment objectives.The next phase involves formulating assessments, designing an instructional strategy, and creating materials to help students demonstrate their proficiency in the objectives.This systematic approach ensures effective learning and development.
